newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin sets spending side of key French 98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Jospin sets spending side of key French 98 budget.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin put the finishing touches on Friday to ministry spending levels for 1998, wrapping up one side of a budget which is crucial to France's preparations for European monetary union.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told reporters after a day of consultations at the prime minister's office on Friday that the spending allocations for each ministry had been agreed, but he declined to give any details.
"The spending side is wrapped up," he told reporters as he left Jospin's office after a day. Details would not be made known before early September, he added.
Each minister is due to receive the final spending limit letter by Tuesday, whereafter the other leg of the highly delicate budget balancing act begins for Jospin's new Socialist-led government.

It must now start working on what the government can expect in terms of revenue next year and the level of economic growth it can hope to secure to help curb its public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in line with its commitment to the euro single currency.

Strauss-Kahn declined to say whether the spending package settled on Friday would limit expenditure rises to a maximum of inflation, forecast at around 1.2 percent, or leave a little more room for manoeuvre.

Government sources said in June Jospin's aim was generally to keep ministers' budget rises to no more than the level of inflation but others sources have more recently suggested the goal could be to set the cap -- a little higher -- at two percent.
If even the upper limit was respected it would amount to a significant cost control exercise, according to UBS economist Erick Muller.
"We have had two messages which look pretty rigorous -- the aim for a three percent public deficit in 1998 and the 1.2 percent (rise) in spending," Muller said.
"If that happens it would be the smallest rise since 1987. It's never been less than two percent since 1987 even if the 1997 budget bill from (former prime minister Alain) Juppe had aimed for lower."

The focus of Jospin's consultations with several ministers on Thursday and Friday was to ensure that the budget allocation was in line with the deficit goal of three percent next year, while rebalancing spending according to new priorities.

The top priority is the employment ministry headed by Jospin's second-in-command, Martine Aubry -- who is in charge of enacting a promise by the new Socialist-led government to create 350,000 jobs for the young in the public sector over the next few years.

Aubry told reporters that talks concerning her share of the budget had "gone well". Following Jospin's talks with several ministers on Friday, she also took part in the deliberations on the overall package, with Jospin and Strauss-Kahn.

Jospin has said the jobs plan, requiring an estimated 10 billion francs ($1.6 billion) in state support next year, will not require new spending and that much of the funding can come from reorganising the already extensive state funds dedicated to help employment.
Other priority ministries are education, culture and justice, while the defence ministry is in the firing line. Defence Minister Alain Richard met Jospin twice on Thursday.
On Friday, Jospin met Education Minister Claude Allegre as well as Culture Minister Catherine Trautmann, and Justice Minister Elizabeth Guigou, who said on leaving that she was "reassured."
Consultations were also concentrating on the biggest budget ministries, education, defence and the interior.
The completed budget bill is due to be presented to the cabinet on September 24.
Jospin's government, which took over in early June after ousting the previous centre-right coalition, plans to turn to the revenue side of the budget in the latter part of August.
Jospin, who had returned from a holiday in the west of France to settle the spending side, returns on holiday until mid-August before the next cabinet meeting on August 20.
The big question now, economists say, is whether he can secure higher non-fiscal receipts and the extent to which he can rely on improved economic growth to boost tax revenues.

The previous government had forecast minimum 2.3 percent GDP growth in 1997 and growth of 2.8 percent in 1998. But economic indicators so far this year have been relatively inconclusive on the timing and strength of a pick-up in the economy.
